resources.string: Crack the hidden code by finding all three digits in the right order. Each guess gives you clues. There is no guess limit: take your time and let logic lead.
Use exactly 3 different digits from 0 to 9. No repeats, in the secret or your guesses. Zero can come first: 012 is a valid code.

R counts digits in the correct place. W counts digits in the secret that belong somewhere else. Winner means all three digits are correctly placed.

In real rounds, every checked tile turns gray. Use the remark counts to deduce the code; gray does not mean a digit is absent.

Only the learning examples use colors: green for a correct place, orange for a wrong place, and gray for an absent digit.
SMYLE means none of your digits are in the secret. It stands for Simply Make Your Life Easy: three digits you can rule out!
For these examples only, the secret is %1$s. In a real game, it stays hidden until you win.
5 is correct in the last place. 2 belongs elsewhere. 3 is not in the secret.
4 is correct in the middle. 5 and 2 are both in the secret, but in the wrong places.
3, 1 and 6 are all absent. None can be part of the answer.
Every digit is in the right place. You cracked it!
Single Player\nThe app picks a random secret. You do the detective work.
Double Player\nA friend enters a secret on Home. The input is masked. Hand the phone to the seeker, who guesses the code using the same rules. Both players share one device.

Tap digits on the keypad. A digit already in your current guess is disabled. DELETE removes the last digit; ENTER checks a complete three-digit guess.

After ENTER, the checked tiles turn gray instead of showing colors. Read the R/W/SMYLE/Winner remark and scroll the board to compare earlier guesses.

The ? button opens this guide without ending your round. Go back to resume. Leaving an unfinished game asks you to confirm quitting.

After winning, HOME returns to setup. Single Player also offers PLAY AGAIN with a new random secret.

Compare the R and W counts across several guesses, not just the last one. Rearrange the same digits to explore positions, or change digits to narrow down which ones belong in the code.

Checked tiles in a real game are all gray, so they do not identify which digits earned R or W. Use the remark counts and earlier guesses together.

A SMYLE row is useful, not a setback. It eliminates three digits. You have unlimited guesses, so experiment at your own pace.
Your mission: find a hidden three-digit code. We will show the practice secret so you can learn how each clue works. In a real round, you will not see it.
From this row, keep 5 at the end and leave 3 out. Since 2 cannot be in the middle and 5 fills the last slot, 2 must go first. The middle digit is still unknown.
Practice secret: %1$s. Enter any three different digits and tap ENTER. Try a few guesses, or enter the secret to see Winner. This practice does not affect a real game.
You cracked the practice code! Ready for a hidden one?
Compare the colors with the practice secret. Try another guess whenever you are ready.

You know the code rules, the clues and the keypad. Unlike these practice examples, real rounds turn every checked tile gray. Use the R/W/SMYLE/Winner remarks to solve the code.\n\nPlay solo now, or go back to Home to set up a game with a friend.

Guesser is simple to learn, but every round invites another thoughtful deduction. Like tic-tac-toe, a small set of rules can open the door to strategy. Notice patterns, remember clues and test possibilities—practice helps you find the code with more confidence, one reasoned step at a time.

In our family, the story of Guesser began long before Wordle became a household name. Its inventor, Paresh Langalia—Keval\'s elder brother and mentor—created the game to play with his children and nurture their curiosity and reasoning.\n\nKeval began the Android project on May 11, 2021. The rules are simple; the challenge is in connecting each clue. Compare your guesses, rule out what cannot fit and let each new hint guide the next. With practice, players can solve more efficiently—not by memorizing a shortcut, but by reasoning through the code.
A quick puzzle to share or solve solo. Each round rewards curiosity, attention and the satisfaction of making a clue click.
Created by Keval Langalia.\nBuilt for Android with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.
